children: By Nat Ives, WSJ Leadership Institute

Welcome back. The Democratic Socialists of America's recent poll successes don't owe entirely to policy positions or candidate charisma, Joshua Chaffin and Maya Davis report for The Wall Street Journal.

DSA organizers are acting like experiential marketers and engaging curious young people with events that are, well, social-like "Coffee With Comrades" in the garden of a Brooklyn coffee shop and "socialist softball" in Queens.
Chapters nationwide offer barbecues, beach days, run clubs, happy hours, karaoke, prom nights and more.
There's even been socialist speed dating. "In the era of late-stage capitalism," a flier read, "our dating and social lives are more and more controlled by for-profit companies."
The New York City chapter built its own onboarding app for new members. In Brooklyn, organizers distribute "Red Cards" with 90-day checklists of activities like attending a coffee or canvassing.
I asked the reporters where this social strategy is coming from.
Do DSA chapters share a "playbook" for these events?

Joshua: My impression from conversations with people at national and local chapters is that this stuff has developed very much in an organic way. Their members tend to be young, and so it's natural for them to link up first on a variety of chats and then through activities. I was told that they didn't study other organizations, like mega-churches, for example, to try to mimic their best practices.

DSA is also a decentralized network with a weak center. The onboarding app is for the NYC DSA and was developed by them. National DSA, meanwhile, has been trying to build a membership portal that would accomplish some of the same goals.
But members are very online and very social. So I think popular ideas-like Socialist Beach Day-pop up on Instagram and the like and get copied by other branches.
Are any other groups or movements taking inspiration?

Maya: Organizations and candidates in the center of the Democratic Party have tried to see how the left's organizing tactics could work for their cause. Covering Congress, I've spoken to moderate lawmakers beginning to experiment with social media hits, door knocking for signatures and grassroots canvassing. I've also followed centrist groups looking to replicate core DSA tactics such as creating chapters.
The extremes of a party are typically the loudest, and the noise has helped groups like DSA grow their energy, especially within Gen Z. It makes other groups think... why not us?
SaasPocalypse, Not Today
Not long ago, Salesforce and other corporate software-as-a-service looked imminently threatened by any-day-now, AI-generated alternatives.
That hasn't happened, Asa Fitch writes this morning for the Journal.

That's partly because writing code is different from maintaining and upgrading established systems. Big SaaS companies are firmly entrenched within customers' IT stacks, frequently through tangled connections with software from rival providers. And the natural drag on complicated change is buying incumbents time to co-opt the AI challenge.

Instead of collapsing, Salesforce last month reported better-than-projected sales and profits, crediting AI for an assist. It also expanded a partnership with Anthropic to weave Claude directly into its platform.

The slightly longer-term peril, then, looks like fresh SaaS companies built from scratch with AI at the core. But the legacy players have strategic moves to make there, too, said Gartner analyst Arun Chandrasekaran, like agreeing to shorter contracts and outcome-based pricing.

For B2B marketers, the takeaway is clear: Defensive moats matter more than ever. And making your customers' lives easier-through seamless daily integration and hands-on upkeep-is the best defense you have.
The Magic Number

Square footage of the shuttered San Francisco Centre, once the city's largest mall and a thriving retail hub anchored by Nordstrom and Bloomingdale's. The property is up for sale, with brokers expecting it to fetch no more than $130 million. That's a staggering plunge from its $1.2 billion valuation a decade ago, underscoring the steep challenges facing brick-and-mortar retail even as AI investment drives a local renaissance.
New Leaders Pod
The latest episode of WSJ Leadership Institute Presents: Leaders could safely be called a friendly interview.

In it, WSJ Leadership Institute President Alan Murray sits down with his boss, Almar Latour, CEO of Dow Jones and publisher of The Wall Street Journal. The two discuss how the company navigates continual media disruption and what's planned for the latest, AI-fueled era of change.

As Alan notes at the start, Almar signs his paychecks. But impartiality aside, the conversation touches on key themes for marketers and executives, including maintaining trust in a polarized society, learning the skills required to be a CEO and keeping a close eye on your customer proposition.

The early internet-era idea that news should be free online showed a "grotesque unawareness of the value of information," according to Almar. Now the early AI era is amplifying the importance of that information.

"You have to be aware that what we're sitting on is not something with diminishing value, it's something that actually has just exploded in value," Almar says. "... You have to understand, what does it mean when a hedge fund uses our information versus when a student uses our information?"
You can watch on wsj.com, or listen on Apple or Spotify.
